statement: Incommensurable magnitudes have not to one another the ratio which a number has to a number.
heath_proof: Let A, B be incommensurable magnitudes; I say that A has not to B the ratio which a number has to a number. For, if A has to B the ratio which a number has to a number, A will be commensurable with B. [X. 6] But it is not; therefore A has not to B the ratio which a number has to a number.
ai_proof_text:
10.7
**Statement:** Incommensurable magnitudes have not to one another the ratio which a number has to a number.

**Step 1.** Let A and B be two incommensurable magnitudes; that is, by definition, A and B cannot have any common measure [D10.1.1].

**Step 2.** I say that A has not to B the ratio which a number has to a number.

**Step 3.** For suppose, if possible, that A has to B the ratio which some number has to some number.

**Step 4.** Then, since the two magnitudes A and B have to one another the ratio which a number has to a number, the magnitudes A and B are commensurable [10.6]; that is, A and B are measured by some common measure [D10.1.1].

**Step 5.** But by hypothesis A and B are incommensurable, so that they cannot have any common measure [D10.1.1]. Thus A and B are both measured by a common measure and cannot have any common measure, which is impossible.

**Step 6.** Therefore the supposition in Step 3 is false; hence A has not to B the ratio which a number has to a number.

Therefore incommensurable magnitudes have not to one another the ratio which a number has to a number. Q.E.D.
